summary:
Legal gender recognition is available across most of Mexico but not all of it. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of the country's 32 states had legislated a procedure for recognising a person's gender identity in official documents, and named six states whose legislatures had enacted none. Zacatecas is not among the six: it operates a legislated route to recognition.

Deputies of the 64th Legislature of Zacatecas approved a reform of the Family Code of Zacatecas on gender identity on 23 December 2022, by 14 votes in favour to 7 against, after the Justice Committee issued a positive opinion (dictamen). The reform establishes the possibility of issuing a new birth certificate recognising an applicant's gender identity, principally for the trans community.

The law has an administrative layer behind it. The Human Rights Watch state-by-state feature of March 2025 records that in 2023 the director of the state Civil Registry issued guidelines implementing the gender-recognition reform, and both the reform entry and the guidelines entry link to the official state gazette of Zacatecas.

Zacatecas's Penal Code also carries an explicit ban on practices aimed at changing gender identity. On 25 August 2021 the Congress of Zacatecas approved the prohibition and sanctioning of conversion therapies, or ECOSIG (Esfuerzos para Corregir la Orientación Sexual e Identidad de Género), by adding fraction VI to article 182 Bis of the Penal Code. Anyone who incites hatred or violence on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or who promotes such practices, faces one to three years' imprisonment or up to 300 days of community work. The same session typified hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity in the Penal Code.

Partnership recognition is settled at the national level: same-sex marriage has been legal across Mexico since 2009.
tangentialFactors:
The recurring finding on Mexican equality law is a gap between statute and practice. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that progressive LGBTQ+ legislation in Mexico is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions explicitly that its earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Human Rights Watch warned on 31 March 2025 that implementation of gender recognition differs sharply from one state to another, and that where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation. Its report of 6 March 2024, "I Just Want to Contribute to Society", documented delays and refusals in Tabasco that leave trans residents carrying documents contradicting their lived identity, with knock-on effects in banking, health care and dealings with police.

Violence against trans people is documented at national scale. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100.

Protection machinery has been activated on the same issue. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels. Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide, taking its name from a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished.
localsOnly:
The gender-identity reform of the Family Code passed the Zacatecas state congress in December 2022 with 14 votes in favour and 7 against, having secured a positive opinion from the Justice Committee first. A gender-identity initiative debated in the same period as a separate constitutional and family-code reform had failed to obtain enough votes and remained pending at that time; the reform itself was approved in December 2022.

Operation of the procedure runs through the state Civil Registry, whose director issued implementing guidelines in 2023. Official texts are published in the state gazette (periodico.zacatecas.gob.mx).

The conversion-therapy ban sits in article 182 Bis, fraction VI of the Penal Code as amended on 25 August 2021, alongside the hate-crime typifications adopted in the same legislative session; the penalty range is one to three years' imprisonment or up to 300 days of community work.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory specifies the practical requirements of the Zacatecas procedure: the documents an applicant must present, any waiting period, fee, residence requirement, or whether a court appearance is needed. Those details are not sourced here.

Processing times, refusal rates and appeal routes for gender-recognition requests in Zacatecas are unresolved. Human Rights Watch records that implementation varies sharply between states, but this inventory does not establish how the Zacatecas procedure performs in practice or whether the 2023 Civil Registry guidelines have been applied uniformly.

No Zacatecas-specific incident of violence against a trans person, and no case under the hate-crime provisions or the conversion-therapy ban, appears in this inventory; enforcement of those provisions in Zacatecas is therefore not sourced.

The count of 22 of 32 states with a legislated procedure is dated 31 March 2025; the current position of the six states named as lacking one, and any legislation adopted after that date, is not sourced here.
